segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. So this is going to be one of those shows where I'm just going to say a few things here and then get out of the way. It's based on a single, kind of a remarkable recording of a thing that happens all over the country, but you never really get to hear it. It's a parole hearing in Illinois-- 13 people in a small room having to decide, should a man be released from prison?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This fact surprised me. Parole hearings, the system where somebody with a long sentence comes before somebody and gets a chance to get out, that's been abolished in about a third of all the states. Most other states have limited it in various ways. The reasons for that-- people in prison and their advocates said it was really subjective, racially biased, unfair. There was no way to appeal the decisions. They said too few people were being set free.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Conservatives, meanwhile, found it too lenient. They said too many people were being set free. So very few people get out of prison thanks to a parole board hearing determining if it's time for their incarceration to end, though right now, there is a lot of talk about expanding the use of parole boards, making more people eligible. There's a bill in the New York State Assembly, two competing bills in Illinois, and they're in other states, too.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Reporter Ben Austen got interested in the question at the heart of all this-- what is actually happening in those parole board hearings? How do they make these monumental decisions? What sways them? What doesn't?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: These boards are trying to adjudicate these very squishy, nearly impossible questions, like when is a person rehabilitated? How can you tell? When should a long prison sentence end? This next question is almost too grand to say out loud, but it is in there, too-- what is justice?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: All this plays out in this weird backwater of the judicial system that doesn't get a lot of scrutiny. Can you remember the last time you saw a news story-- any news story-- about a parole board hearing? And for all the TV dramas about-- I have to say-- almost every aspect of the criminal justice system in all of its parts, there is none set in a parole board.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Ben lives in Illinois and spent more than a year going to every parole board hearing there. They happen once a month, each one looking at 5 or 10 cases. And he put together what you're about to hear.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The man they're considering for release in this case is 72 years old, been locked up for almost 50 years-- most of his life. The parole board has some information about the case, but definitely not everything you would want. That's part of what makes it so interesting listening to this, hearing how they deal with that.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is actually one of the hearings that Ben sat through on his very first day going to these hearings. Basically, he and his producer, Bill Healy, showed up, threw two recorders on the table in the middle of the room, and captured this conversation that you're about to hear.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And it just stuck with him, this case-- not just the difficulty of the decision that they had to make or all the stuff that they wished they knew but didn't know, but the ruling they came to stuck with him. OK, enough said. Here's Ben Austen.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: I'm surprised by how plain the hearing room is, how small. There's barely enough space to fit a wood conference table. And squeezed around it, 13 board members are sitting elbow to elbow. These are people who spend a lot of time together. They're from different parts of the state. And in between the cases, they debate things like who has worse traffic, worse snow.

segments.speaker: Perkins
segments.text: You guys don't get it like we get it in Peoria.

segments.speaker: Perkins
segments.text: (SUBJECT) BOARD MEMBER 1: I don't know. We're still about 50 miles south.

segments.speaker: Perkins
segments.text: Yeah, you don't get it.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: They tease each other about being long-winded.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: (SUBJECT) BOARD MEMBER 2: Keep it short, Vonetta. Remember that.

segments.speaker: Vonetta
segments.text: Oh, look at you tell me to keep it short. Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: Vonetta
segments.text: (SUBJECT) BOARD MEMBER 2: Who said that?

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: They hunch over laptops and coffee cups and fat accordion files filled with case documents that go back way into the previous century. There's a former public school principal and a high school guidance counselor, former prosecutors, and three retired cops.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: By law, the parole board includes both Democrats and Republicans. They're appointed by the governor, approved by the state senate. And it's a full-time job in Illinois. They're currently paid about $100,000 a year.

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: OK, the next case is Mr. Henry Dee. Ms. Martinez is recognized.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: The hearing starts. The chairman acknowledges Virginia Martinez, one of the board members. She's seated near the head of the table. And she begins to talk about the person they're considering for release.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: This is the case of Henry Dee, number C01657. Mr. Dee is currently 72 years of age, having been born on August 24, 1946. I interviewed him at Stateville Correctional Center.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: If you look around the small conference room, one person you won't see is Henry Dee, the guy up for parole. He's still in a prison more than 100 miles away. The way these hearings work, one board member travels to the prison and interviews the parole applicant. The pairings are chosen at random. It was Martinez's turn.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: Now, she'll walk her colleagues through the details of the case and what she learned in the interview. And she'll give a recommendation for or against Dee's release. The other board members don't have to follow it. Often, they don't. They'll debate, and after that, they'll vote. The whole thing takes less than an hour, and for some cases, way less.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: Inmate Dee is serving 100 to 200 years for two counts of murder to run consecutively and 20 to 40 years for two counts of robbery. His projected discharge date is June 27, 2162.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: Martinez says the release date is 2162. Dee was given up to 200 years. It's what people in prison call "Buck Rogers time," like out of science fiction. Henry Dee-- that's his last name, D-E-E-- first came before the parole board in 1981. People who are rejected get another hearing every one to five years. And Dee has had two dozen hearings since.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: To make parole, you need a majority of the board's votes. Dee has never even come close. In fact, in all his years of coming up for consideration, only one board member has ever voted for release. That's it-- just one. A big reason-- the severity of the long-ago crime.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: The facts of the case-- in the early morning of August 17, 1971, cab driver Arthur Snyder stopped at his Chicago home after his evening shift. He was accosted by inmate Dee and co-defendant James Sayles, who were armed and forced their way into the Snyders' apartment.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: The details-- they're painful to listen to. The crime is brutal. If you're listening with kids, this is a heads-up.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: Once inside, the offenders hogtied, gagged, and blindfolded Arthur Snyder, leaving him in the kitchen. They then took Edith Snyder into the bedroom, where they bound, gagged, and blindfolded her.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: This was a robbery. The men stole some valuables. And then--

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: The offenders then beat her to death with a claw hammer, brutally striking her about the face, skull, and body. They then returned to the kitchen, where they beat Arthur Snyder with the same hammer, striking him so hard that the hammer became embedded in his skull.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: Mr. Snyder was 52 and his wife was 46 at the time of their murders. Before leaving with a number of items taken from the apartment, the offenders turned on the gas jets in the oven and set the mattress on fire where Mrs. Snyder's body was laying.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: There was evidence of rape, but no charges were brought. They stole Arthur Snyder's car, his taxi, and drove off. All this information is from Dee's original trial. But listening to it in this room, it feels present tense, like these terrible events just happened. You quickly lose sight that this took place in 1971, that a half century has passed.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: The inmate and co-defendant were tried together, found guilty in a jury trial. The verdict was affirmed on appeal.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: In considering release, board members weigh different factors-- public safety, the suffering of victims. One of the most important things they want to hear is that the parole candidate feels remorse, that they're repentant, that in prison, they've changed, which is a big problem for Henry Dee, because he insists he can't say he's sorry-- another reason he's only ever gotten one vote in a couple of dozen parole hearings.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: The inmate's version is that he states and has always stated that he's innocent, that he's never killed anyone. He states that the blood that was found on his clothing was a minute amount, so small that it could only be tested once. He had tried to get the blood tested again, and they told him that was impossible.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: He claims that he had given a palm print that didn't match the bloody print on the hammer and that that evidence has disappeared. He said he was never in the cab. He had gotten a call to meet Sayles and went to Sayles' South Side apartment.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: Sayles is James Sayles, the other person charged with this crime. Dee says he met Sayles at a writers' workshop. They became friends. They volunteered together at a free breakfast program run by the Black Panthers. So that night, Dee says, they were hanging out at Sayles' apartment.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: Then later, Sayles was walking inmate back to the train. That is when they were arrested.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: The cab driver and his wife were white and lived on Chicago's North Side. Henry Dee and James Sayles were Black and lived miles away on the city's South Side. The taxi was found later on the South Side, but Dee says he and his friend had nothing to do with it. The police arrested the wrong guys, framed them. He's been saying the same thing for 48 years.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: At the trial, the inmate, Dee, did testify, and he testified that he and Sayles left Sayles' apartment at about 2:35 AM and were crossing 62nd Street when they had to hurry to avoid a speeding car. Moments later, they were called over to a police car and questioned as to their identity and activities in the area.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: He testified that the police then took both Sayles and he to a cab parked in Washington Park. They both denied any knowledge of the cab. According to inmate Dee's testimony, they were kicked and beaten by the police. The police then took items out of the cab and threw them on the ground. The police also added whatever the two had in their pockets to the same pile.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: OK. So Dee says the police took them to the cab, planted evidence on them, and beat them. The police say they saw them running from the cab. At trial, a doctor undercut Dee's version of events.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: A doctor testified at trial that the two had not said anything about being beaten and did not observe any recent injuries or bruises on the defendants at the time of their arrest. The inmate states that everyone he has asked to look into the case has said they can't because there is no DNA and everyone involved in the case is dead. He said he could have pled guilty and was offered 20 to 40 years, but he didn't take it because he's innocent. He believes he would have been out by now.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: So what to believe after all these years-- Henry Dee's version or the police version? A parole hearing isn't a trial. These 13 people are not here to decide whether Henry Dee is innocent or guilty. Parole was set up to assess everything that's happened since a conviction. But of course, as the board wrestles with accountability and remorse, it's impossible to ignore that question of guilt. What if he never committed the crime? How could he show regret?

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: Another thing the board is supposed to consider-- the person's behavior in prison. How has he conducted himself there for the past half century? Has he used the time productively? Short answer-- yes, he has. That's where Virginia Martinez goes next. Henry Dee has basically been what they call a model prisoner, with two rather spectacular exceptions. These floored me when I heard them. First one--

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: In 1979, inmate Dee escaped from custody of the Department of Corrections while at the U of I Hospital for kidney tests.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: That's right. He escaped from prison. This was early in his incarceration.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: He was able to do so by using what looked like a homemade weapon. He stated that he handcuffed the two officers and left the keys and their weapons in the trash can so that when someone went in, they could uncuff them. He was apprehended the next day at a motel with his girlfriend.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: It's a crazy story. He made a fake gun, like a stage prop, and when he locked up the officers, he was polite. He didn't take their guns. He left them, along with the keys, somewhere easy to find. He wasn't even charged with a crime, though they did punish him by moving him out of the general prison population for a year. It's hard to gauge how this will play with the parole board, especially since, a year later, Henry Dee tried again-- another attempted escape.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: He tried to walk away from MCC, the Metropolitan Corrections Center, while he was downtown in federal court on a civil rights case that I think he and others had filed, which he said he won. So he tried to walk away, and the federal marshals caught and then charged him. So he's got a three-year sentence on that.

segments.speaker: Pete Fisher
segments.text: So he won and lost?

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Pete Fisher
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: Mm-hmm, yes.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: A board member makes a joke that Dee won and lost. The man's name is Pete Fisher. He's white, bald, a former police chief from Central Illinois.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: During his time on the board, he's voted against parole, like, 200 times, and for release in only a couple of cases. He tells me later, when I interview him, that what always matters most to him is the severity of the crime, no matter how much time has passed or how much someone has accomplished in prison.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: Virginia Martinez goes on to describe Henry Dee's accomplishments. After those escape attempts in 1979 and 1980, she sees someone doing about as well in prison as anyone could hope.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: In the past 30 years, inmate's overall adjustment has been very positive. He has received only four tickets.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: Tickets are disciplinary infractions. And having just four of them over all that time is extraordinary.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: He's currently assigned to the dietary department and has previously worked in correctional industries, receiving certifications for working with sheet metal, which is where I think he made this-- what looked like a gun. He makes file cabinets and other metal furniture. He has also worked in the canning plant. He has never posed a threat to others, except for the use of what looked like this weapon to escape.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: In 1983, his attitude was described as energetic, friendly, and cooperative. In 1984, inmate's institutional adjustment was described as remarkable. Since 1998, the words "model prisoner" have been used.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: Because Henry Dee isn't there, he's like a distant character in all the stories swirling about. He's turned into less a person than some abstraction of crime and punishment. But Martinez now gets to say what it was like to sit with him in the present, to talk with him, to get a sense of who he is today, at age 72. He's got a lot of health issues.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: The inmate is insulin-dependent and also suffers from hypertension, hyperactive thyroid, and abnormal heart rhythm. He recently underwent-- I think it's a second surgery for his heart condition. When I interviewed him, his speech was slow and clear. He was very cooperative and responsive to questions. He had come with his accordion file of information. He keeps all of his information in a file.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: For people Henry Dee's age-- older than 65-- the arrest rate is really low. Statistically, people age out of crime. That's just a fact. But the board still wants to know, if they do release him, that he's got a stable place to live, an income, a plan.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: His parole plan, he has always said that he wants to live with his mother, Ruby, in Chicago. She's got to be in her 90s. He says over 85, but that over 85 has been consistent over the years, so she's got to be 90-something. She requires a caretaker now.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: He has been saving money for his and her needs and currently has over $11,000. He believes that he can get work in either food service or sheet metal based on his experience and certifications. Additionally, we received a letter at the end of January of an offer from Juan Rivera, a former Stateville inmate who was found to have been wrongfully convicted and won a $20 million civil rights suit based on that wrongful conviction.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: Mr. Rivera states that inmate Dee is, in great part, responsible for the person he is today. He met inmate Dee while he entered Stateville, angry for having been convicted of the rape and murder of an 11-year-old girl, a crime that he did not commit.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: He says inmate Dee taught him that he was not who the legal system portrayed him to be. He is now owner of Legacy Barber College and is a director of Justice for Just Us, a nonprofit providing support for innocent people who are exonerated and released from prison. He offered inmate Dee a place to live in his home, a job with the Barber College, and whatever he needs.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: Martinez is done presenting the case to her 12 colleagues around the table. The other board members will get a chance to ask questions and deliberate before there's a vote. I can't even tell at this point how Martinez is going to vote. But right now, she says, there are people who sent letters to the board who continue to oppose release. I don't know if it's the victims' family members or who. She doesn't say.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: I would ask that we go into executive session to discuss.

segments.speaker: Donald Shelton
segments.text: I'll second.

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: OK, we'll go in close. We'll excuse our visitors for a few minutes as we discuss protests.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: The board chairman asks us to pick up our recorders from the table so they can discuss the protests in a closed session.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: And we go in the hallway and wait.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Ben Austen. Coming up, the members of the parole board puzzle through everything you just heard, all the pros and cons of whether Henry Dee should go free, and they cast their votes. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Today's program, "This is the Case of Henry Dee," the story of a single parole hearing for a man who was incarcerated since he was 24 years old. At the time of the hearing, he's 72 years old.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So here's where we are. The parole board members have heard about the crime. They've heard about how Henry Dee has used his years in prison. Now, they have to discuss and decide, should he be allowed out? Again, here's Ben Austen.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: The board members take their seats again and settle in. They have to decide whether, after 48 years behind bars, after this terrible crime, that some unquantifiable measure of justice has finally been served. There's Henry Dee's incredible record in prison, too, and also his two escapes.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: And then there's Dee's assertion that he's innocent. It's maybe the biggest hurdle to voting for him. Innocence at this point calls into question the work, in the past, of police, prosecutors, judges, and, also, all those parole boards dating back to the 1980s. All of them would have needed to get it wrong.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: As I mentioned, the co-defendant in this case was paroled in 2004.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: The hearing resumes. Virginia Martinez now has to give her recommendation for or against Henry Dee's release from prison. How to decide? Martinez previously worked in nonprofits representing women and children and American Latinos. She was actually one of the first two Latino lawyers ever to be licensed in Illinois, in 1975.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: As far as how often people on this board vote for release, Martinez is somewhere in the middle. She sometimes talks about her fears of making what she calls a mistake, recommending someone for parole who goes on to commit another crime. And the crime in this case, she told me later, it gave her nightmares. But she now tells her colleagues, she's open to the idea that Henry Dee might be telling the truth and police, prosecutors, judges, and previous parole boards might have gotten it wrong.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: I found it hard to believe that these two men convicted of what is absolutely-- has to be one of the most brutal and barbaric murders that we have, that they never exhibited any violence while incarcerated at Stateville, which you all know about. Even when they lost their appeal, an event that the psychiatrist and counselors predicted would set them off, neither became violent.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: Inmate Dee did escape and was disciplined. He wasn't charged with the IDOC escape. He did not harm the officers and did not take their weapons. In the federal case, he tried to walk away-- again, no violence. His release would show other inmates that there is hope.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: I believe inmate Dee is ready to reenter society. He has saved money, and he has a financial and other support from Juan Rivera. His institutional record, age, and physical health would be an indicator that he's not likely to re-offend.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: It's clear-- Martinez is going to vote for release, only Henry Dee's second vote ever. The board members now get to ask questions.

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: Colleagues?

segments.speaker: Donald Shelton
segments.text: Well, I don't want to get into retrying it, but you've had the case. You've had the file. Is it your belief that he's innocent? Just curious.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: I don't know whether he is or he isn't. I think it's possible.

segments.speaker: Perkins
segments.text: You think it's possible he could be innocent?

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: Yes. I mean, he had another case of an excellent record. He says he completely-- Sayles says he completely changed himself. Mr. Dee has completely changed--

segments.speaker: Donald Shelton
segments.text: [INAUDIBLE]

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: --whoever he was--

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: (SUBJECT) BOARD MEMBER 3: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: --at the time. I mean, he's now 73 years old. And if part of the goal of the Department of Corrections is to rehabilitate individuals, here is a person who has been rehabilitated.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: Even if he is guilty and won't admit it, she's saying that whatever we think a long prison sentence is supposed to accomplish, after 48 years, he's done it. They should set him free.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: This gets at something so basic-- what is the purpose of punishment? It's a question we, as a country, have never really answered. And yet it's here for the board somehow to wrestle with.

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: Mr. Ruggiero.

segments.speaker: Joseph Ruggiero
segments.text: I just have a couple questions in regard just to the actual innocence claim. The victim, Mr. Snyder, owned the cab, correct?

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Joseph Ruggiero
segments.text: And--

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: Another board member seated a couple of feet from Martinez, Joseph Ruggiero. He's white, a criminal prosecutor for 30 years. And he starts to grill Martinez about the crime like he's got her on the witness stand.

segments.speaker: Joseph Ruggiero
segments.text: And was Dee, according to the opinion, found in possession of the victim's watch?

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: No, I think he had certificates or something. But again, Dee says that this stuff was inside the cab.

segments.speaker: Joseph Ruggiero
segments.text: And wasn't Dee found in possession of an 1893 buffalo head nickel that belonged to the victim?

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: There were some things that they found on him and some things that they found on Sayles. That's what they said.

segments.speaker: Joseph Ruggiero
segments.text: And his criminal history, twice earlier that year-- two separate occasions-- he was charged with stealing a car, correct? This would have been the third time he was in a stolen car?

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: Ruggiero seems like a clear no vote. Next board member with questions-- Donald Shelton, a police officer from downstate, the only Black Republican on the board. And he also wants to revisit the police account of this arrest, which dates back to when Richard Nixon was president.

segments.speaker: Donald Shelton
segments.text: In my mind, there's a small vacuum in my understanding how they came to be arrested. The police saw this vehicle driving dark. The car pulled over, and these guys got out of the car. Is that right?

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Donald Shelton
segments.text: Were they arrested in the vicinity of the car? Had they crossed the park? Were they on the other side of town? I don't understand--

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: He said--

segments.speaker: Donald Shelton
segments.text: --how they connected them to the car.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: I don't know the South Side well enough to know where the parking lot to the swimming pool of-- I think that's where it was. It was near the swimming pool of Washington Park where they parked and then ran.

segments.speaker: Lisa Daniels
segments.text: So that's on Cottage Grove. Go ahead.

segments.speaker: Donald Shelton
segments.text: That's what I'm just trying to figure out, where they got stopped in relation to the car, because that's kind of--

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: It was near-- it was near--

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: Compared to courtrooms, parole hearings can feel like there are no rules. This was one of the reasons many states abolished it. Suddenly, here they are, debating the layout of Washington Park, something they could just look up on their phones.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: It's unclear what any of this is getting them. The trial wrapped two generations ago. There's no new evidence. And no one in this room was involved in the case. If this were a retrial, there would at least be witnesses, evidence. But here, it's just circling the same old court documents.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: And even if he is guilty, that's who parole is for, right? People who were found guilty, rightly or wrongly. To decide whether, today, they're ready to rejoin society. But like in so many hearings I've seen, the board members again travel back in time to the original conviction.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: So they were convicted.

segments.speaker: Donald Shelton
segments.text: I get that. That's why we're sitting here.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: So I'm not arguing about-- he says he was innocent.

segments.speaker: Johnson
segments.text: Ms. Martinez, you mentioned he claims he's innocent. OK, has that remained consistent over the years?

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Johnson
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: Absolutely yes.

segments.speaker: Johnson
segments.text: And he's had appeals--

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: He never said anything.

segments.speaker: Johnson
segments.text: --and he's had other things, and that's all exhausted. OK. Was there any-- with your interview of him, was there any remorse on his part? Or I guess it's hard to have remorse if you're thinking--

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: Exactly. He just said, I have never killed anybody. I didn't do this. I have never killed anybody.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: Next, visitors are allowed to speak in support of parole or against it. Sometimes, it's relatives of the victims. Their testimony is almost always crushing. I remember one guy. His father had been killed when he was a child. He told me how hard it was to live with that, then to have to come back here every few years and hear the details of the crime again and again.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: Other visitors include the lawyers for the parole candidates or their family members. But that's not the case today. Relatives of Arthur and Edith Snyder, the couple who was killed, aren't here. And Henry Dee doesn't have any family here either. He doesn't even have a pro bono lawyer.

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: Ms. Futorian, are you here to speak for Mr. Dee?

segments.speaker: Aviva Futorian
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: Please.

segments.speaker: Aviva Futorian
segments.text: Only because he doesn't have a lawyer. And I'm not representing him, but--

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: But you are a lawyer.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: The woman who responds is sitting right next to me. Her name's Aviva Futorian. She's in her 80s, and she advocates for parole candidates in Illinois, meeting with them in prison, trying to improve their chances.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: For years, she attended nearly all of these hearings, writing up notes and sharing them in a newsletter. So the board chairman turns to her and asks, does she have anything that might offer some insight? It turns out, she does.

segments.speaker: Aviva Futorian
segments.text: A while ago, I was at Stateville, and one of the correctional officers came up to me and said he was a big fan of Henry Dee's. And he knew Henry was claiming he was innocent. And he said, could you talk to him about this? And tell him that if he doesn't admit it, he may never get out.

segments.speaker: Aviva Futorian
segments.text: And that's what I did. I put in a legal call to him, and I told him who I was. And I told him that I thought that there was a good chance he would not get out if he didn't acknowledge his guilt.

segments.speaker: Aviva Futorian
segments.text: And he said, I understand that. I know that. And if it means I have to stay in for the rest of my life, I can't admit to something I didn't do. So that's the only insight I can add to it, was my conversation with him.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: Next, the board chair calls on a state's attorney from the county where the crime occurred. There's someone like this at nearly every hearing I saw. She's there to say why the prosecution still opposes release after 48 years. But she has no connection to the case. I'm nearly certain no one from her office has spoken to Henry Dee in the decades since the trial.

segments.speaker: State's Attorney
segments.text: So I understand that it may sound like a sympathetic story of somebody who's claiming that they're innocent, but the fact of the matter is, is he stands convicted of this brutal, heinous double homicide. The appellate court reviewed the evidence that was presented and found that the conviction should be affirmed. And that's what happened.

segments.speaker: State's Attorney
segments.text: This is not the place to talk about actual innocence. I think him denying this would deprecate the seriousness of the offense. Granting him parole would also do that. And I ask that you deny parole.

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: It's almost time for the vote. So far, only one of the 13 board members has said they support release. Another board member speaks up, Sal Diaz. He's seated by the door because he showed up last. He's a former Chicago cop, old-school. He's wearing a tracksuit. He says he knows that in Chicago, there are a lot of documented cases of false arrest.

segments.speaker: Sal Diaz
segments.text: The state's attorney says that he was convicted, but we all know some convictions, even though they were on the appellate level, are bogus, OK? We understand that. And I'm a former policeman. I've seen that over and over again. Bad arrests. But he had the victim's property on him.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: That's what the police say.

segments.speaker: Sal Diaz
segments.text: That's what he said.

segments.speaker: Donald Shelton
segments.text: But even some of that property is property that would have been in the cab--

segments.speaker: Donald Shelton
segments.text: (SUBJECT) BOARD MEMBER 4: In the cab.

segments.speaker: Donald Shelton
segments.text: --not--

segments.speaker: Donald Shelton
segments.text: (SUBJECT) BOARD MEMBER 5: Right.

segments.speaker: Donald Shelton
segments.text: --on the victim.

segments.speaker: Donald Shelton
segments.text: (SUBJECT) BOARD MEMBER 5: On the victim.

segments.speaker: Donald Shelton
segments.text: So--

segments.speaker: Donald Shelton
segments.text: (SUBJECT) BOARD MEMBER 5: OK.

segments.speaker: Donald Shelton
segments.text: So there's some--

segments.speaker: Sal Diaz
segments.text: And if the police--

segments.speaker: Sal Diaz
segments.text: (SUBJECT) BOARD MEMBER 5: Yeah, and if they dumped it all on the floor, all out.

segments.speaker: Sal Diaz
segments.text: Simply because the police chase people doesn't mean that the police are lying when they catch them. You know, it can be 50-50.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: 50-50? Those seem like terrible odds the police might be lying. Still, Diaz says he'd be more ready to vote for parole if Henry Dee just hadn't said he was innocent.

segments.speaker: Sal Diaz
segments.text: I wish, for me, he would have said, no comment, as opposed to, I'm innocent. And that would have made me feel a little more comfortable.

segments.speaker: Sal Diaz
segments.text: At the same time, he's done a lot of good work. And Martinez has pled his case very well. And sometimes, I think we have to just say, hey, there may be some doubts here. I like the guy. He's impressed me. But he needs to go home. And I understand that. And that's all I'm going to say.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: At first, Diaz seemed like a definite no. Now, I'm not so sure. The chairman, Craig Findley, has been on the board longer than anyone else. He's a former state legislator, a moderate Republican. He says he's also troubled that Henry Dee never accepted responsibility for the crime.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: The other man arrested with Henry Dee eventually did. Initially, James Sayles also said he was innocent. Their stories lined up. Then after years in prison, Sayles admitted he was guilty, that they did the crime. And after that, he got paroled.

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: Voting to parole Mr. Sayles was probably the most difficult vote I ever cast. It was probably in 2005 or 2006.

segments.speaker: Sal Diaz
segments.text: Yeah, it was '05, but--

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: Yeah, that was probably my most difficult vote at the time because of the gruesome nature of the crime. Ms. Futorian, correct me if I'm wrong, but it seems to me Mr. Sayles not only admitted his own guilt, but indicated that Mr. Dee was his co-defendant. Much as I would like to support Mr. Dee, I'm troubled to consider paroling him.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: The chairman looks like another no vote for parole. There's often a randomness to these hearings. Sometimes, the outcome seems like it's 100% certain, and then a board member will offer a stray comment, and it swings the momentum in the opposite direction.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: There's a board member who's barely spoken today, Lisa Daniels. She's Black, in her 50s. Tattooed on one of her forearms are the words "I am forgiveness."

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: At these hearings, she'll occasionally bring up how her own son was murdered. He was trying to rob another young man in a drug deal when he was shot. She'll mention this to stress that her son shouldn't be summed up by one terrible moment, that nobody should. And right now, she says she wants to share a theory.

segments.speaker: Lisa Daniels
segments.text: Can I ask something or offer something for consideration? Ms. Futorian mentioned earlier that Mr. Dee was told that if he did not acknowledge--

segments.speaker: Lisa Daniels
segments.text: (SUBJECT) BOARD MEMBER 6: I was just going to say that.

segments.speaker: Lisa Daniels
segments.text: --committing the crime, that he would never be paroled. Maybe we want to take into consideration that Mr. Sayles took that advice, that Mr. Sayles was given that same advice and that he took it.

segments.speaker: Lisa Daniels
segments.text: (SUBJECT) BOARD MEMBER 7: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Lisa Daniels
segments.text: (SUBJECT) BOARD MEMBER 6: That's exactly what I was going to say.

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: That's a rational assumption to make.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: It's like something in the room shifts. I see a few heads nodding. People are agreeing.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: (SUBJECT) BOARD MEMBER 6: We don't know. We'll never know.

segments.speaker: Lisa Daniels
segments.text: I mean, we don't know, and we'll never know. But--

segments.speaker: Lisa Daniels
segments.text: (SUBJECT) BOARD MEMBER 7: Right.

segments.speaker: Lisa Daniels
segments.text: --I would like to offer it as a consideration.

segments.speaker: Sal Diaz
segments.text: I asked him that-- Sayles. He said no. He said no. We brought it up. But he didn't point a finger at that.

segments.speaker: Lisa Daniels
segments.text: And just one more thing. The reason I brought that up is because what I'm not hearing-- and maybe Ms. Martinez can speak to that-- is that typically, when someone changes, completely changes their behavior and their mindset, there's a point.

segments.speaker: Lisa Daniels
segments.text: There's a religious conversion. There's some sort of eye-opening, life-altering event that changes a person. And I'm not hearing that that took place for either one of these gentlemen throughout their period of incarceration.

segments.speaker: Lisa Daniels
segments.text: And so my mind is wondering, how is it that people-- how is it that these two men could have committed such a violent, violent, heinous crime, but then moved on to live a life of peace or such a peaceful existence without some point of turn?

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: That's my question, too. How could these two individuals who, at Stateville, have such an incredible record, and not only for themselves, but for Dee to be a mediator-- which the counselors tell us, too. They mediate the fights between inmates, as well as between the staff and the inmates. How could somebody who-- these were horrible, horrible murders.

segments.speaker: Lisa Daniels
segments.text: Yeah, we got-- yeah.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: I mean, the pictures are there. They're horrible. But how could that-- and especially when even the psychiatrist said, oh, yeah, but if they don't win their appeal, they're going to go off. No, they lost their appeal, and they didn't. They didn't go crazy. They didn't cause any problems in the institution.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: There really is no way to prove any of this, that someone who commits a terrible act of violence couldn't go on and live a life of peace, other than a feeling.

segments.speaker: Johnson
segments.text: Has he had prior counsel?

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: Not for us, I don't think. He had the same counsel with Sayles for the appeal, but after that, I don't think he's had an attorney.

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: I don't think he's ever been represented before, but he's been eligible for parole--

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: --previously--

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: --for a very long time.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: 1981, he came before us for the first time. In all that time, he's gotten one vote. And there was, actually, also a statement in one of those decisions about, he needed a little more time. You have it now.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: But it was '83-- it might have been later-- that the board said he needed a little more time. He's had it. He's had 46 years. I believe that he's been rehabilitated. And I believe that he presents an acceptable risk. And so I move that we--

segments.speaker: Perkins
segments.text: Overruled. Did you say--

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: Oh, first, is there a second of the motion?

segments.speaker: Harris
segments.text: Second.

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: Ms. Harris. Ms. Perkins.

segments.speaker: Perkins
segments.text: Did you say he just had four tickets in--

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: 30 years.

segments.speaker: Lisa Daniels
segments.text: Four tickets in 30 years.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: At Stateville. At Stateville. I keep thinking about that.

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: Easy place to get tickets.

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Perkins
segments.text: Yeah. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: And then after this discussion that zigged and zagged, suddenly, the conversation's over. It's finally time. The board members will cast their votes. Henry Dee needs eight yeses to get parole, a majority of the 14-member board. This is even harder today because one of the board members is absent. He still needs eight votes, though. Those are the rules.

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: All right. Any further discussion? Hearing none, the motion is to grant an aye, yes vote as to grant parole to Mr. Henry Dee. Please take the roll.

segments.speaker: Samantha
segments.text: Ms. Martinez?

segments.speaker: Virginia Martinez
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Samantha
segments.text: Mr. Norton?

segments.speaker: Norton
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Samantha
segments.text: Ms. Perkins?

segments.speaker: Perkins
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Samantha
segments.text: Mr. Ruggiero?

segments.speaker: Joseph Ruggiero
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Samantha
segments.text: Mr. Shelton?

segments.speaker: Donald Shelton
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Samantha
segments.text: Mr. Tuby?

segments.speaker: Tuby
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Samantha
segments.text: Ms. Wilson?

segments.speaker: Wilson
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Samantha
segments.text: Ms. Daniels?

segments.speaker: Lisa Daniels
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Samantha
segments.text: Mr. Diaz?

segments.speaker: Sal Diaz
segments.text: I think he's dirty, but I'm going to vote for him.

segments.speaker: Sal Diaz
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: Sal Diaz, the Chicago cop, certainly not soft on crime, says he's dirty. He still thinks Henry Dee is guilty. But, he shrugs, he'll vote for him anyway.

segments.speaker: Samantha
segments.text: Mr. Dunn?

segments.speaker: Dunn
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Lisa Daniels
segments.text: Is that a yes?

segments.speaker: Samantha
segments.text: Ms. Harris?

segments.speaker: Harris
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Harris
segments.text: [AUDIBLE GASP]

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: You can hear a gasp from someone in the room because that was the eighth vote.

segments.speaker: Samantha
segments.text: Chairman Findley?

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: I'll go with Sal. Yes. Dirty as the day is long.

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: [? (SUBJECT) DONALD SHELTON: ?] Thank you. He made it.

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: But please read the result. He did receive eight votes. Is that correct?

segments.speaker: Samantha
segments.text: Nine.

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: Nine votes.

segments.speaker: Samantha
segments.text: Nine votes.

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: The board order parole will be granted-- do we need 90 days, Samantha?

segments.speaker: Samantha
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Craig Findley
segments.text: 90 days from today, the--

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: After 48 years of incarceration, Henry Dee was going free. The whole thing took less than an hour. Of the seven cases the board considers today, this is the only one granted release, and I can't stop thinking about it. It's all my producer, Bill, and I talk about on the three-hour drive back from Springfield to Chicago, because we just saw a long prison sentence end. It's impossible to sit through these hearings and not think about what decision you would make.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: For me, there's no question-- I would have voted for release. And I want to be clear about what it means to say that, because two people were murdered, and I don't think we'll ever know what happened. I'm saying that even if Henry Dee did kill Edith and Arthur Snyder back in 1971 and lied about it all these years, even then, to me, it was time to let Henry Dee out. Past time.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: We spent a long time trying to get in touch with the family of Edith and Arthur Snyder. I did eventually reach their daughter. She's now about 80 years old. She told me she strongly opposed Dee's release, had written a letter to the board before this hearing and for nearly every one of his hearings over the years. She believes he's guilty. And she says, even if you're a saint in prison, if you take a life, it's forever. So you should never be let out.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: We talked for a while about parole, about our different views on punishment. She said, had your loved ones been killed, maybe you'd feel the same way I do. I told her that was a fair point. I still believe what I believe, but it's true. I haven't gone through what she has.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: I didn't say this earlier, but Illinois is one of the states that got rid of parole, way back in 1978. So only people like Henry Dee, sentenced before 1978, are still eligible for hearings like this one. So the people who come before this board are mostly in their 60s and above. They're senior citizens, which means, on any actuarial table, they pose very little risk of committing another crime. And still, the parole board only says yes to a tiny percentage-- in the 15 years before Dee's hearing, just 6% of them.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: So who makes the cut? In the numerous cases I've seen, the people who did get released, there's always a story that enough board members were able to latch onto, something that allowed them, finally, to move beyond that magnetic pull of the long-ago crime. In Henry Dee's case, it was the unbridgeable distance between the brutality of the murders and the peacefulness of his life in prison.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: Another guy I saw get paroled, he had a surgery that left him bleeding in his cell for years. The horror of his medical care in prison made his offense seem to the board almost beside the point.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: And then this other time, a man not only escaped, but lived under an alias in a different state for years. He was a beloved member of that community before he was apprehended again. The board, to my shock, saw that time when he was at large like a test case for the positive life he'd live if they gave him another chance.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: I've thought a lot about whether Illinois and the rest of the country should bring back parole, whether it makes sense to get more people in front of boards again. Parole decisions can be racially biased, completely focused on the original crime, and just random.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: But even knowing all this, I think we need more systems of second chances. The United States locks up more people than any other country, about one in six of all the incarcerated people in the world. There are hundreds of thousands of people in prisons like Henry Dee. They've spent decades behind bars. Many will die there. They deserve another look.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When we come back, Ben tries to track down Henry Dee. That's in a minute, from Chicago Public Radio, when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Ben Austen picks up the story again.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: Even after sitting through Henry Dee's parole hearing, I didn't really know him. I hadn't even seen or heard him. So I tried to find out more. Here's what I learned.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: After Henry Dee makes parole, people at the prison celebrate, even the staff. And the day he walks out the front gate, he's getting hugs and congratulations from everyone. His mother's still alive, in her 90s. She's not walking. She can't meet him there. But Henry is ecstatic to see her.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: He gets outside-- his first free air in 48 years-- and there are federal officers waiting for him. They handcuff him, put him in a car. Henry has no idea what's going on. He eventually learns it's for one of the attempted escapes all those decades ago. He's been granted parole by the state, but the feds are tacking on two more years. He's driven to a federal prison in Pennsylvania. His mom dies during that time.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: 27 months later, the feds put him on a plane to Chicago. He's never flown before, has no idea how to board, where to sit. The flight attendants learn his story and move him to first class. He has to turn down the free drinks because he doesn't want to violate his parole.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: From O'Hare, he gets on a train. He's got directions written out on paper. He doesn't have a cell phone. He makes it to a Salvation Army on the city's West Side. That's where he sleeps. He later moves to a homeless shelter. The friend from inside who won the wrongful conviction suit who promised Henry a job and a home, it doesn't pan out.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: So Henry's trying to figure out his new surroundings, his new life, but he has medical issues. Eventually, he's admitted to the hospital. He has diabetes, fluid on his lungs. And after a few days there, he's dead. Henry Dee was incarcerated for 50 years. He lives free after his release for less than 12 months.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: I tracked down a few people who knew Henry Dee well. I want to take these last few minutes to tell you some things about him. Henry Dee wore a frog pin around the prison. He'd leave the cell house, walk onto the yard, and dozens of stray cats would appear. He'd feed them. He was a large man, hands like catcher's mitts. When young guys asked him who his gang chief was, he'd tell them his mom.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: Because of his diabetes, he could get jittery or pass out on the toilet in his cell, and his friends were always on watch for him. For nine years, the person who lived with him in a six by eight foot cell was a guy named Jacob Rivera.

segments.speaker: Jacob Rivera
segments.text: Henry was funny, man. I would sit in a cell on lockdowns and write these letters. And not having a very good educational background, whoever I was writing to, I tried to make it seem like I was educated. And I would try to use these big words.

segments.speaker: Jacob Rivera
segments.text: And I told Henry-- hey, Henry, what word can I use for blah, blah, blah, blah, blah? He's like, what are you trying to say? And then I would tell him what I was trying to say, and he'll say, well, just say that. [LAUGHS] You know? And I'm like, oh, yeah. Yeah, he had a way.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: Jacob called him Grandpa. A chaplain at the prison told me she called him Father Abraham because she saw him as a man of wisdom and love. Those times he came up for parole, the entire prison felt hope. Here's another man who was locked up with him, Andre Ruddock.

segments.speaker: Andre Ruddock
segments.text: All of the guards, all of the officers, all the way up to the warden, everybody would get engaged. Like, everybody knew, Henry Dee goes to the board. He's going to the board. They might let him out, finally. This might be his year.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: When Henry Dee finally got released, Andre was already out. And when he learned that Henry was sleeping in a homeless shelter, he was furious. So Andre raced over to the shelter, called some people, and they got Henry Dee an apartment. They recorded a video of him seeing it for the first time. Here he is, Henry Dee.

segments.speaker: Woman 1
segments.text: That's your living room, all right?

segments.speaker: Henry Dee
segments.text: Yeah, that's my living room.

segments.speaker: Woman 1
segments.text: This is your little kitchen area.

segments.speaker: Henry Dee
segments.text: Ooh, Lord.

segments.speaker: Woman 1
segments.text: You got a brand-new bathroom.

segments.speaker: Henry Dee
segments.text: A brand-new bathroom! Wow.

segments.speaker: Woman 2
segments.text: This is nice.

segments.speaker: Andre Ruddock
segments.text: Look at it.

segments.speaker: Henry Dee
segments.text: Well, this is wonderful. This is more room than I done had in the last century.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: Henry has a full white beard. He's wearing a wool hat and a gray hoodie. And he uses a walker as he enters the remodeled kitchen. There are granite countertops. Everything is bright and freshly painted. Henry is jubilant. They all are.

segments.speaker: Andre Ruddock
segments.text: Come look at your bathroom.

segments.speaker: Henry Dee
segments.text: Man, I see it all from right here.

segments.speaker: Henry Dee
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Henry Dee
segments.text: I've been living in a bathroom smaller than this all my life. Whew, look at that.

segments.speaker: Woman 1
segments.text: Hopefully, you'll enjoy your space.

segments.speaker: Henry Dee
segments.text: Oh, I do. I enjoy it already.

segments.speaker: Andre Ruddock
segments.text: Nice.

segments.speaker: Henry Dee
segments.text: You've done a wonderful job. Thank you so much. What's your name?

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: Henry had 351 days of freedom. I saw a video of him from one of those days. He's surrounded by three little dogs leaping all over him, and he's giddy. He loved to play the lottery. And he had this new makeshift family-- the people who knew him in prison who now just wanted to be around him.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: But he never slept in the new apartment. At night, he'd go back to the homeless shelter. For five decades, he'd been surrounded by hundreds of people. He was terrified of being alone. Andre told me that in prison, Henry was a giant.

segments.speaker: Andre Ruddock
segments.text: After all that, after all that he survived, he was a powerhouse. This is what we all knew. Henry Dee was so big. And he talk about his hands big. He had this deep, powerful voice. This was the character.

segments.speaker: Andre Ruddock
segments.text: But then he came home, and the real world shrunk him. It shrunk him and then defeated him. And he never got a chance to do anything that he really wanted to do. And one of the things he told me when he was in the hospital, that he wanted to go to the observation deck on Willis Tower.

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: The Willis Tower, also known as the Sears Tower, is Chicago's tallest building.

segments.speaker: Andre Ruddock
segments.text: I told him that's the first thing we're going to do when you get out of the hospital. I'm going to take you up there. But since he died, he obviously couldn't. So I took his picture that you have, that obituary. I took it up to the observation deck and took a picture of it. [CRYING] Like, yeah, Henry Dee, you made it. We got you up here, so. [CLEARS THROAT]

segments.speaker: Ben Austen
segments.text: As far as I can tell, Henry Dee out of prison was the same person Virginia Martinez saw in prison, the same person prison officials had been describing to the parole board for decades.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Ben Austen. He wrote a book about the parole system and the odysseys of two men trying to go free. It's called Correction.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He also hosts a new podcast called The Parole Room, which centers around a different case than the one you just heard-- a kind of famous case in Chicago, actually-- with lots of twists and turns, including a guy on parole who gets out and then insists on attending parole hearings with Ben.
